title: Supercharging Think, Pair, Share
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton takes the familiar Think, Pair, Share routine and argues that, while sound, it is usually run in a way that squanders its benefits. He rebuilds it as a seven-step sequence that makes student thinking visible at every stage. The first move is protecting the Think phase: Barton draws on Bjork's retrieval research and Mary Budd-Rowe's wait-time work to show that cutting thinking time short lowers accuracy and hands the paired discussion to the quicker student. He then threads mini-whiteboards through the whole routine, using them to capture independent answers, as a shared object in the paired discussion, and as a record of what students changed. The key innovation, borrowed from Craig Latmir, is giving students a chance to rewrite after discussion and then Warm Calling those who did, which turns the Share phase from random selection into a strategic surfacing of misconceptions. The piece is a practical pedagogy guide grounded in retrieval and formative-assessment research.
points: Barton identifies the most common failure of Think, Pair, Share as teachers truncating the Think stage, which denies students the benefits of effortful retrieval and lets the faster partner dominate the pair.
Writing answers on mini-whiteboards before pairing is presented as a cognitive-load move: students need not hold their idea in memory while also attending to their partner.

A whole-class board check after the Think stage gives a baseline of what students know alone, and practical tactics (row-by-row reveals, checking weaker students first, final answer on the reverse) make it workable with complex questions.
Structured pair prompts, comparing boards, deciding who is right, or crafting the best explanation, keep the Pair stage purposeful rather than open-ended chat.
Letting students rewrite after discussion, then Warm Calling those who changed their answers, converts the Share stage into a targeted exploration of misconceptions.
quotes: A common thing I see in the classrooms I am lucky enough to visit - and I know I did this myself loads! - is the teacher asks a question, and no sooner have they uttered the final syllable, they ask students to turn to their partner to discuss the answer. In other words, they cut short the Think part of Think, Pair, Share.

We know from the work of Bjork and others that the act of trying to retrieve knowledge is beneficial as it makes that knowledge more secure and available. With less time to think hard about an answer, students do not enjoy the benefits that such effortful retrieval brings.

It can help students organise their thoughts, reflect on their thinking, and make changes. Writing things down also improves the paired discussion that follows because students do not need to try to remember what they wanted to say whilst also trying to attend to what their partner is saying.

It is a good idea to get a sense of what students know before they have the opportunity to collaborate. Eliciting such information after the Think stage shows us what students know on their own, serving as a baseline before we embark upon the Pair and Share stages.

Finally, even if we cannot analyse each and every one of our students’ answers, the fact we ask them to write something down and then see what they have written gives us a check for effort. If students have not written anything, we are aware of this and can follow up to find out why.

If our mini-whiteboard check reveals all students understand the question, there may be no need for a paired discussion. Instead, we could jump straight to asking students to share their reasoning or offering an explanation ourselves.

We can ask the students we noticed doing a rewrite: what they originally thought the answer was, what they changed it to, and why they made the change. This may reveal a misconception or misunderstanding that we want to discuss explicitly with the class.
